papers.title: Reversion to the Meta Body Form of Life after Complete Cell Death in Pure Liquid Water
papers.abstract: The prevailing view holds that simpler animate beings predating the dawn of cellular life once existed, yet they have long since vanished from the present-day Earth. Our hypothesis posits that these animate beings persist to this day. To this end, we devised a long-term experiment spanning over a decade, keeping Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus) within a sealed aqueous system of pure water. The findings illustrated that, upon the complete cell death (CCD) of the S. aureus, as cellular remnants progressively succumbed to dissolution, the aqueous solution underwent self-purification, bringing forth a class of lipid bilayer membrane microspheres containing RNA and proteins. These structures maintained long-term sustainable stability within the thermodynamic storm of water molecules and underwent dynamic size fluctuations over time - collectively exhibited phenomena indicative of being "alive". This study reveals that the cell, upon complete cell death, undergoes reversion to a living entity simpler than the cell itself - the Meta Body (MB). The discovery of MB opens an entire re-conceptualization of what death ultimately brings.

papers.title: TRF2 mediates force-resistant bridging of distal telomeric DNA repeats
papers.abstract: Shelterin binds telomeres, regulates telomere length, and protects chromosome ends from mis-repair, which is essential for genome stability. Telomere end-protection uniquely depends on the TRF2 subunit, which assembles telomeric DNA into a protective T-loop structure in vivo, yet the biochemical mechanism underlying this process remains unresolved. Using single-molecule optical tweezers and atomic force microscopy, we show that the human shelterin complex tethers distal telomeric DNA repeats, looping the intervening DNA. These bridges withstand tens of piconewtons of applied load, rupture at a force that scales with telomeric repeat number and re-form on relaxation. Structure-function analysis demonstrates that this force-resistant tethering is TRF2-dependent under our conditions and depends on multiple interfaces, with the TRFH domain making a major but non-exclusive contribution: introducing the TRF2 TRFH domain into TRF1 is sufficient to confer tethering, whereas its deletion from TRF2 reduces but does not abolish activity. We propose telomeric dsDNA tethering by TRF2 as a candidate first step in T-loop formation, preceding invasion of the telomeric 3' ssDNA overhang.

papers.title: Linker stretching optimizes bonding entropy in sticker-spacer condensates
papers.abstract: Phase separating biopolymers are often described by the sticker-spacer model, which accounts for non-attractive linkers that connect discrete attractive moieties. "Associative polymer" theories describe these systems as two coexisting fluids of stickers and spacers, respectively. In such theories the stickers and spacers are decoupled in the sense that sticker binding does not affect spacer conformations or vice versa. Informed by coarse-grained simulations, we develop a phenomenological mean-field theory to determine the microscopic coupling between the sticker and spacer degrees of freedom. Accounting for linkers connecting adjacent spacers introduces free energy contributions due to conformational entropy of the spacer and the binding combinatorics of the stickers. These contributions have opposite dependencies on spacer length because longer spacers allow a greater volume to search for binding partners but incur a greater entropy cost upon bond formation. The length dependent terms from these contributions cancel leaving a length-independent elastic term arising from the fact that a small amount of spacer stretching lowers the free energy by increasing the number of possible binding partners. The cancellation of spacer length from the theory justifies the decoupling approximation and supports mean-field treatments of heterogeneous spacers.

papers.title: Latent-Space Residue-Pair Networks from Molecular Dynamics Distinguish Ligand-Activated and SAVI-Associated STING
papers.abstract: Stimulator of interferon genes (STING) provides an informative model system for developing methods to extract and compare residue-pair fluctuation patterns from molecular dynamics (MD) trajectories. We combined a one-dimensional convolutional autoencoder trained on apo STING with temporal mean pooling, Mahalanobis-distance clustering, and residue-pair similarity networks to compare apo, ligand-bound, and SAVI-associated multi-mutant datasets using 25-dimensional latent descriptors. Networks constructed from clusters capturing state-dependent fluctuation patterns showed lid-dominated organization in the ligand-bound dataset and a1b1-enriched, structurally distributed relationships involving residue 281 in the multi-mutant dataset. These findings identify contrasting residue-pair fluctuation signatures in the analyzed trajectories and provide an interpretable framework for generating hypotheses about ligand-associated and mutation-associated dynamic allostery.

papers.title: Buried Ion-Pairs Reshape Folding Pathways of Artificial Proteins
papers.abstract: Ion-pairs are central charged motifs that control the biological function of several proteins. Yet, the physical principles linked to the formation of ion-pairs during protein folding remain poorly understood. Here, we show that buried ion-pairs of de novo-designed helical bundle proteins reshape the folding pathways by introducing kinetic barriers that are overcome by a hydrophobic collapse linked to packing of the protein core. By combining protein design with co-translational folding studies, nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy, and molecular dynamics simulations, we show that introduction of a buried ion-pair leads to a shifted folding transition that balances desolvation and electrostatic interactions within the protein and the bulk solvent. Moreover, we find that the folding pathway is sensitive to modifications in non-polar interactions and motifs that electrostatically shield the ion-pair from its surroundings. Our combined findings provide a blueprint for understanding how functional motifs affect protein folding and how mutation of charged networks alter the stability of proteins.

papers.title: Chain-Length-Dependent Interactions of Polyethylene Nanoplastics with Human Catalase reveals Size based Nanoplastic Toxicity
papers.abstract: Nanoplastic contamination is increasingly recognized as a biochemical stressor, yet the molecular determinants governing how polymer fragment size dictates protein-level interactions remain poorly understood. Here, we combine molecular docking and all-atom molecular dynamics simulations to characterize the interaction of polyethylene (PE) oligomers of increasing length (n = 3, 5, 7, and 14 repeat units) with human catalase, a tetrameric heme enzyme central to cellular antioxidant defense. Single-chain simulations reveal that short PE fragments (3-, 5-, and 7-mer) migrate from an initial domain-connector pose toward a heme-proximal, previously characterized inhibitor-binding site, whereas the 14-mer remains kinetically confined to a peripheral surface site, implicating short-chain PE as a potential catalase inhibitor. In multichain corona systems, backbone dynamics show a non-monotonic, chain-length-dependent destabilization, with the 3- and 5-mer inducing the greatest structural perturbation and the 14-mer best preserving native-like dynamics despite forming an extensive, percolating surface network across all four subunits. MM-PBSA free energy decomposition identifies van der Waals interactions as the dominant thermodynamic driver of binding, while electrostatic surface mapping indicates that cationic surface patches instead govern long-range spatial targeting of PE chains. These findings establish a framework linking nanoplastic fragment size to protein-level toxicity, with direct implications for assessing the biochemical risk of environmentally weathered polyethylene.

papers.title: Autofocusing molecular simulations for integrative structural biology of broad conformational ensembles
papers.abstract: Integrative structural biology seeks molecular descriptions consistent with complementary experimental measurements. A particular challenge arises for molecules whose broad conformational ensembles resist description by a few representative structures, such as natively unfolded proteins and fluid-phase biomembrane lipids. Although molecular simulations can generate such ensembles, their simultaneous agreement with a large number of experimental constraints is commonly prevented by model inaccuracies. Here we introduce autofocusing as an approach that integrates experimental information by automated finetuning of the physical model generating the ensemble. We demonstrate it for a fluid bilayer of the phospholipid POPC, for which no existing force field has simultaneously reproduced the complete set of 82 NMR C-H bond order parameters. Autofocusing brings all the 82 within experimental uncertainty while preserving agreement with independent small-angle X-ray scattering measurements and retaining or improving agreement with untargeted NMR relaxation rates and effective correlation times, thus supporting its description of membrane structure and dynamics beyond the calibration targets. The resulting simulations challenge a long-standing two-state interpretation of phosphatidylcholine headgroup structure, instead supporting a broad conformational ensemble poorly represented by crystal-derived conformers. These results establish autofocusing as a practical approach to constructing experimentally grounded conformational ensembles while retaining the computational tractability of classical molecular dynamics.

papers.title: De Novo Design of Flavoproteins with Controlled Excited State Dynamics
papers.abstract: Designing photochemical properties in proteins is a frontier challenge in biomolecular design, which, when realised, will open new avenues in catalysis and biomolecular electronics. Here we demonstrate an integrated computational design framework, supported by ultrafast spectroscopy, combining protein design, quantum mechanical/molecular mechanics molecular dynamics (QM/MM MD) and electronic structure calculations, to control flavin excited states in de novo proteins. Iterative design yields FC-4D2, a flavocytochrome with covalently bound flavin and non-covalently bound heme B and Fl-4D2, where the heme-binding site is removed. Both proteins are highly thermostable, and access all physiologically relevant flavin redox and protonation states, while high-resolution X-ray crystallography confirms the near-[A]ngstrom-level accuracy in design. Incorporating QM/MM MD and linear-response time-dependent density functional theory (LR-TDDFT) into the design workflow enables engineering of a flavin-tryptophan charge-transfer variant, Fl-4D2CT, that modifies the flavin absorption spectrum, substantially alters its redox properties and suppresses fluorescence. Ultrafast studies reveal how protein design reshapes the excited state relaxation timescale and mechanism. Our study establishes a modular strategy for programming flavin photochemistry in designed proteins.

papers.title: A Geometrical Class of Population Growth Models, across Scales and Population Structures
papers.abstract: We develop a general geometrical framework for growth processes in which the growth rate depends exponentially on the number of active growth-supporting components. The framework separates the fraction of active components from the size of the accessible component space, allowing qualitatively different growth laws to arise from the same underlying construction. Bacterial population growth provides an example of a fixed-size component space controlled primarily by activation and deactivation, whereas examples such as human population growth or speciation provide an expanding component space in which interactions between individuals promote further growth. This motivates a Replicative geometrical law, dX/dt= X exp({beta} X^{gamma}), whose exponent characterizes the scaling of the effective growth-supporting component space and is tested against historical human-population regimes and eukaryotic lineage-through-time data. For innovation indicators such as patents and arXiv manuscript submissions, where an existing item need not itself reproduce, the same construction motivates a Direct Geometrical production law without the prefactor X. The framework therefore provides a common description of fixed and expanding component spaces while distinguishing Replicative from Direct Geometrical growth.

papers.title: A modular DNA toolkit for single-molecule biophysics
papers.abstract: Long, customizable DNA molecules are an essential tool for in vitro single-molecule biophysics. Most studies still rely on the {lambda}-phage genome, which has a fixed sequence, a non-uniform GC distribution, and limited options for modification. To overcome these limitations, we developed a modular DNA (ModDNA) toolkit that integrates in silico sequence design with cloning, to create long (up to 100 kb) DNA molecules with entirely user-defined sequences. We used a computational workflow with curated databases to design a motif-depleted sequence backbone, into which any desired sequence can be inserted at any position. Golden Gate assembly then builds these sequences into constructs, which we extend iteratively in defined increments up to 100 kb. We show precise placement of local features, e.g. a fluorophore, a bound protein, and a DNA-origami structure, and illustrate the construct's utility in single-molecule visualization assays, including DNA loop extrusion by human condensin I. ModDNA offers a scalable, sequence-programmable alternative to {lambda}-DNA and other restrictive substrates. More broadly, the motif-aware feature-free design connects single-molecule biophysics to emerging efforts in machine-guided regulatory-sequence design and synthetic-genome engineering, where controlled programmable sequence context is increasingly essential.

papers.title: Transcription factor interactions promote binding to non-cognate DNA sites
papers.abstract: Recruitment of transcription factors (TFs) to non-cognate DNA sequences is widely observed, but the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we show that, within the nucleosome, Sox2 can bind an Oct4 motif, interact with the Oct4 POU-specific domain, and displace the Oct4 homeodomain. We also observe Sox2 binding at multiple near-canonical and non-canonical DNA sites, with these interactions promoted by a second Sox2 molecule or by nearby nucleosome-bound Oct4. The TF-TF interactions can bridge across DNA gyres, bringing together binding sites that are distant in linear DNA but spatially proximal on the nucleosome. We further find that Sox2 can engage across nucleosomal DNA gyres through loop regions and/or intrinsically disordered segments, providing an additional mode of chromatin binding. Together, our structural and biochemical data reveal how TF-TF interactions change DNA recognition on the nucleosome, enabling binding to non-cognate sequences and expanding the repertoire of pioneer factor interactions on chromatin.

papers.title: Fusion Peptide Insertion Configuration Determines the Mechanism of Membrane Curvature Induction in Human Parainfluenza Virus Type 3
papers.abstract: Viral entry requires remodeling the host membrane with a short fusion peptide (FP) that anchors and deforms the target lipid bilayer. However, the contribution of the FP throughout the full fusion pathway remains unknown. Here, all-atom molecular dynamics simulations define the membrane- deformation mechanisms associated with two distinct insertion configurations of membrane-bound human parainfluenza virus type 3 (HPIV3) FP. Molecular simulations quantifying the linear response of curvature to the peptide are complemented with analyses of lipid organization and FP-lipid interactions to define the underlying membrane-deformation mechanisms. The surface-parallel FP configuration generates positive membrane curvature through deformation of the proximal leaflet, consistent with the classical hydrophobic insertion (wedging) mechanism. In contrast, the transmembrane FP configuration generates curvature through localized deformation of the distal leaflet, a distinct mechanism that would strongly influence later stages of fusion. Cryo-electron tomography shows that target membrane curvature at virus-host contact sites is consistent with the molecular dynamics prediction. In the absence of F-protein activation and FP insertion, the cryo-ET-determined curvature distribution shifts toward negative values, thereby isolating the role of the fusion protein in inducing early-stage curvature that enables the host and virus membranes to approach one another. Modeling key mutational changes isolates how aromatic and electrostatic interactions act together to promote curvature generation. Taken together, these findings establish FP insertion configuration as a determinant of productive membrane curvature across the full fusion pathway.

papers.title: Modeling centrosome positioning by actin--microtubule crosstalk and actin anchoring at the cell membrane
papers.abstract: Centrosome positioning is governed by mechanical interactions between the actin and microtubule cytoskeletons, yet the contribution of different actin architectures and their attachment to the cell membrane remains unclear. We use numerical simulations to study a centrosomal array of microtubules interacting with cortical, bulk, and centrosome-associated actin networks, including passive cross-linkers, motor proteins, and ERM-mediated coupling of actin to the cell membrane. We find that bulk and centrosome-associated actin alone are insufficient for robust centrosome centering, whereas sufficiently dense cortical actin promotes centering through steric interactions with growing microtubules. ERM-mediated attachment of cortical actin to the cell membrane enhances this effect, allowing stable centering at lower actin densities. In a two-centrosome system, microtubule interactions generate a spindle-like structure, while the organization of actin and its membrane attachment through ERM regulate centrosome separation. Antagonistic microtubule motors further limit centrosome separation and establish a finite spindle length. These results demonstrate that ERM-mediated coupling of actin to the cell membrane provides an important mechanical link between the actin cortex and microtubule-driven centrosome positioning, influencing both centrosome centering and spindle geometry.

papers.title: Frustration Quenching and Network Topology of the Energy Landscape as Primary Determinants of Protein-Ligand Binding Pose Prediction by Deep Learning Models
papers.abstract: Deep learning co-folding and docking models accurately predict ligand binding poses at orthosteric sites yet systematically underperform at allosteric pockets. Here, we demonstrate that this accuracy gap reflects a fundamental biophysical property of local energy landscape topology specifically, the magnitude of frustration quenching upon ligand binding rather than an intrinsic algorithmic defect. By evaluating leading co-folding and docking paradigms across curated benchmarks and large-scale uncurated datasets, we show that AI prediction success strongly tracks frustration quenching which the degree to which ligand binding relieves local energetic strain to form a steep energy funnel. Topologically, frustration-weighted residue interaction networks reveal that orthosteric pockets act as high-betweenness communication hubs embedded within contiguous, minimally frustrated pathways. In contrast, allosteric sites reside in low-betweenness peripheral regions with fragmented frustration profiles, presenting flatter, entropy-dominated landscapes that challenge structure prediction algorithms. Comparing generative diffusion with single-shot regression demonstrates that multi-pose sampling capacity is required to cross energy barriers and discover the frustration funnel, whereas joint receptor-ligand coordinate co-adaptation governs local optimization within the funnel. Collectively, this study reframes the allosteric "blind spot" as a quantitative property of energy landscape architecture rather than a defect of any specific predictive framework. We demonstrate that frustration quenching magnitude and structural network centrality serve as physical descriptors that define the intrinsic limits of AI performance, reframing AI accuracy from a benchmark metric into a physics-grounded quantitative reporter of macromolecular binding landscape architecture.

papers.title: Structural thermodynamics by cryo-EM resolves minute energy differences in heterogeneous protein complexes.
papers.abstract: Hetero-oligomeric protein complexes play crucial roles across biology, providing combinatorial diversity and context-specific functionality in membrane receptors, molecular chaperones and beyond. Yet, existing methods are limited in their ability to resolve and quantify the assembly energetics of complex biomolecular populations. Here, we introduce a comprehensive method combining iterative 3D classification, error-rate quantification via simulated particles, and global thermodynamic modeling to extract interaction energies from cryo-EM data. Using hexameric cruciferin (the primary rapeseed storage protein) as a model, we reconstruct a 1.83 [A] structure and distinguish three highly similar 50 kDa isoforms. We resolve the complex compositional heterogeneity of the hexameric species at the single-particle level and fit a global binding model revealing pairwise interaction energies between isoforms differing by fractions of the thermal energy (kB T ). This method offers a powerful, broadly applicable tool to characterize the compositional heterogeneity and energetics of biomolecular complexes.

papers.title: Small-Molecule Inhibitors Allosterically Control Bruton's Tyrosine Kinase Assembly on the Membrane
papers.abstract: Bruton's tyrosine kinase (Btk) is the target of small-molecule, active site inhibitors for treatment of lymphomas and leukemias. Beyond its catalytic activity, Btk participates in signaling assemblies through scaffolding functions that can contribute to drug resistance. Here, we show that Btk forms micron-scale assemblies on membranes and that this behavior is allosterically controlled by ligand binding at the active site. Using supported lipid bilayers and total internal reflection fluorescence microscopy, we find that nucleotides and inhibitors including ibrutinib, acalabrutinib, and dasatinib promote assembly, whereas fenebrutinib and pirtobrutinib prevent assembly. Membrane organization is independent of catalysis but correlates with ligand-dependent changes in Btk conformational flexibility measured by hydrogen-deuterium exchange. These results reveal a previously unrecognized connection between active-site ligand binding and mesoscale membrane organization, demonstrating that kinase inhibitors can control Btk behavior beyond suppression of catalytic activity.

papers.title: Modelling the formation of skin ulcers observed in Buruli ulcer disease
papers.abstract: Buruli ulcer (BU) is a neglected tropical skin disease caused by infection with Mycobacterium ulcerans. The mode of its transmission into the skin has not been fully clarified, but it is believed to involve mechanical transfer, perhaps by insect bites. M. ulcerans secretes a toxin called mycolactone which causes necrosis of the skin and formation of large skin lesions. Understanding the development of these skin lesions over time is crucial to understand the pathogenesis of BU. We formulate a mathematical model to describe the space-time dynamics of M. ulcerans bacteria, mycolactone and skin cell densities as well as fibrin deposition. We investigate the relative contributions to ulcer formation of direct cytotoxicity of mycolactone and ischaemia following the loss of coagulation control. Our results are consistent with existing biological evidence that higher mycolactone concentrations accelerate cell death. Furthermore, the model indicates that the rate of wound expansion is primarily controlled by the diffusion and net birth rate of bacteria, which sets the overall scaling for the speed of wound expansion, along with two dimensionless constants that define the shape of the trajectory of wound edge position against time, namely the ratio of the mycolactone diffusion coefficient to the bacterial diffusion coefficient, and the ratio of the mycolactone degradation rate to the bacterial net birth rate. When mycolactone diffuses significantly faster than bacteria spread or when mycolactone degrades more slowly than bacteria reproduce, the initial development of the wound is faster. In contrast, the long-term wound expansion speed appears to be relatively unchanged across a wide range of the dimensionless parameters.

papers.title: Sample-efficient time-resolved X-ray crystallography with serial small wedges
papers.abstract: Time-resolved crystallography can be inaccessible for membrane proteins and other difficult-to-crystallize targets for which suitable crystals are scarce. Here we present an acquisition strategy that records consecutive diffraction images during a small crystal rotation synchronized to a single activation pulse. Matching image segments are merged across crystals to reconstruct successive time windows, enabling a single crystal ensemble to capture an extended structural trajectory. Using the Mesh&Collect workflow at a synchrotron, we obtained ten consecutive 7.5-ms time windows at 2 [A] resolution from 1,255 microcrystals of a bacteriorhodopsin triple mutant at room temperature. An additional 790 crystals extended the observation window to 500 ms. Rotation-based processing, retrospective time binning and dose control maximize information extracted from each crystal, while compatible measurements can be pooled across acquisitions. This approach makes millisecond time-resolved crystallography practical for crystal-limited targets at synchrotrons, with further development potentially extending the temporal resolution down to 1 ms.

papers.title: Single molecule Grb2 dynamics reveal spatiomechanical modulation of RTK signaling across length scales
papers.abstract: Extracellular matrix (ECM)-mediated cell adhesion and tension regulate development and disease through crosstalk with Receptor Tyrosine Kinases (RTKs). RTKs stimulate proliferation, survival, and metabolic reprogramming via Ras/ERK and PI3K/Akt signaling. Emerging evidence identify the biophysical and biochemical integration of integrin-mediated adhesions with RTK signaling, however, the molecular mechanisms regulating this phenotype remain poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that ECM stiffness potentiates ligand-mediated epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) signaling at scales ranging from the single adaptor protein, Grb2 upward to multicellular spheroids and tissues. We show that ECM stiffness-driven RTK signaling is mediated by integrin adhesions that reshape the membrane to induce the formation of RTK signaling hotspots distributed globally across the cell membrane. A parsimonious computational model and biochemical membrane perturbations causally implicate membrane curvature and topography in tension-dependent integrin-EGFR crosstalk. The results demonstrate how the mechanical properties of the ECM direct molecular recruitment and confinement of signaling molecules to regulate growth factor-dependent RTK signaling. Given that many RTK-driven solid tumors develop a stiff stroma, the findings could explain why many therapeutic tyrosine kinase inhibitors develop clinical resistance. The findings suggest clarifying how tension regulates transmembrane receptor signaling could identify unique force-dependent molecular regulators towards which new antitumor therapies could be applied.

papers.title: Senescence-induced Spatio-temporal Re-organization of the Nuclear Lamina Dynamic Landscape at Single-molecule Level in Live Human RPE Cells
papers.abstract: A defining hallmark of cellular senescence is the extensive remodeling of the nuclear lamina (NL) in both structure, composition, and its interactions with lamina-associated genomic domains. However, how such senescence-induced changes could quantitatively impact the spatio-temporal dynamics of NL interactions at the single-molecule level remain poorly understood. Herein, using human retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells as model system, we establish a robust, chemically inducible cellular senescence model capable of recapitulating key signatures of the senescence-associated phenotype. Senescent RPE cells exhibit distinct alteration patterns in the expression of various NL components, including lamin B receptor (LBR) and emerin, two key mediators of NL-chromatin interactions. Importantly, live-cell diffusion measurements via imaging FCS reveal globally enhanced mobility for both LBR and emerin, indicative of weakened NL anchoring in senescent cells. Single-molecule tracking and super-resolved STAR mapping further unveil distinct, multi-modal re-organization of their NL-binding dynamics in both space and time (especially in the form of LBR binding "hotspots" where multiple stable binding events cluster to effect more extended and prolonged interaction), in line with their respective expression-level alterations and differential lamin interactions. Moreover, correlative mapping uncovers a strong spatial coupling between reduced LBR mobility and highly condensed constitutive heterochromatin domains at the NL, which become dispersed during senescence. Collectively, these findings demonstrate the re-organization of NL dynamic landscape at single-molecule level as a critical and previously under-explored facet of senescence-induced NL remodeling, and point to a synergistic interplay between physical de-anchoring, dynamic attenuation of stable NL-binding and spatial restructuring of chromatin architecture in modulating NL-heterochromatin contacts to potentially effect global changes in senescence-associated gene expression.

papers.title: SCKAnalyzer: A Web Tool for Single-Cycle Kinetics Analysis and Simulation
papers.abstract: Surface plasmon resonance (SPR) and biolayer interferometry (BLI) are well-established label-free analytical technologies used to determine biomolecular interaction rates (ka, kd) and equilibrium constants (KD). While assays historically rely on multi-cycle kinetics (MCK), this approach requires intermediate surface regeneration, risking sensor degradation and increasing reagent consumption. Single-cycle kinetics (SCK) avoids regeneration by sequentially injecting increasing analyte concentrations. However, implementing SCK workflows on biosensor platforms like the OctetRR8 BLI instrument (Sartorius) remains a challenge due to the lack of built-in or online data analysis tools. To address this, we introduce SCKAnalyzer, a free, user-friendly web application designed for processing and fitting SCK datasets. SCKAnalyzer accepts column-based text files and native raw BLI data (.frd format) from Sartorius instruments, performing data pre-processing and non-linear fitting to a 1:1 interaction model. Additionally, it offers advanced simulation capabilities that allow variable association and dissociation durations across sequential injection steps, a feature absent in existing platforms such as BiacoreTMSimul8. The performance of SCKAnalyzer was experimentally validated using a 3-step SCK method (SCK3) for DNA/RNA duplex formation on a Biacore T200, as well as 4-step (SCK4) and 5-step (SCK5) methods for DNA/DNA duplex formation on an OctetRR8 BLI instrument. Binding parameters (ka, kd, KD) derived from SCKAnalyzer showed excellent agreement with values from established proprietary softwares such as Biacore T200 Evaluation Software v3.2.1 and BIAevaluation v4.1.1. SCKAnalyzer provides a practical alternative to MCK, reducing probe consumption and extending SCK utility across biosensor platforms. SCKAnalyzer is available at sck.iecb.u-bordeaux.fr (source code: github.com/synthaze/sckanalyzer).

papers.title: Blockiness as Determinant of Liquid Phase Formation by Polypeptide-Like Polymers in Stickers-Spacers Paradigm
papers.abstract: Liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) driven by intrinsically disordered protein regions underlies the formation of membraneless organelles. The role of these structures in cell biology is an active area of research, yet their physical understanding remains less developed than that of protein assemblies with well-defined, rigid tertiary structures. The amino acid composition of disordered regions, particularly the abundance of charged residues, is known to modulate phase behavior. These factors govern accessible conformations, the assembly of compact sticker clusters, and the porosity of the resulting polymer networks. In contrast, the spatial distribution of side-chain volumes remains a comparatively understudied sequence determinant. Here, we employ a model that captures the patterning of side-chain volumes and interaction strengths without specifying chemical identity to show how sequence blockiness modulates the phase-nucleation propensity, connectivity, and compactness of polypeptide-like polymer assemblies. Using a library of polymers with identical composition but permuted residue arrangements, we show that clustering of bulky residues generates cooperative sticker domains and identify the threshold blockiness required to stabilize polymer networks. Coarse-grained simulations and mean-field theory reveal that this effect arises from an interplay among steric repulsion, solvent entropy, and higher-valency interactions, whereby blocky patterns promote the formation of multi-node percolated networks. Segregation of stickers and spacers is therefore one of the sequence parameters governing LLPS which may be useful for interpreting the evolution of disordered protein sequences, high-throughput proteome screening, and engineering of stimuli-responsive biomaterials. These rules may be exploited to predetermine condensate stability, viscoelasticity, and molecular exchange rates without altering chemical functionality.

papers.title: Anneal-MaxCal: kinetic ensembles from a Markov model learned along a solute-tempering ladder
papers.abstract: A full characterisation of a molecular system requires its metastable states, their populations and their interconversion rates. Molecular Dynamics can in principle provide this characterisation but is limited by sampling and by force-field inaccuracies. Enhanced sampling addresses the first problem, but typically requires prior knowledge of reaction coordinates or metastable states and often sacrifices the kinetics, while maximum-caliber reweighting by Brotzakis, Vendruscolo and Bolhuis [Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. U.S.A., 118(2):e2012423118, 2021] has been implemented to that matter on reweighting continuous pathways by imposing rate constants as kinetic constraints in two-state protein folding. Here, we introduce Anneal-MaxCal, which tackles both problems by imposing rate constants or time-resolved data on a Markov model learned along an annealed solute-tempering ladder spanning softer to physical interactions. MBAR assigns physical free energies to all 160 cells of a slow TICA subspace, against 79 visited at the physical coupling. The square-root approximation (SqRA), a discretised diffusion on this free-energy landscape, converts these populations into a detailed-balance rate matrix. Its prefactors, which act as a position-dependent diffusivity across each cell face, are learned from transitions at the softer couplings and extrapolated log-linearly to the physical coupling. This yields rates and a committor across the TICA space, although the physical rung contains a single barrier crossing. For alanine dipeptide, 665 ns of simulation give a relaxation time of 5430 {+/-} 996 ps against 4413 {+/-} 446 ps from 15.4 s of unbiased dynamics, whereas a constant prefactor is 2.5 times too slow. Maximum caliber then minimally perturbs this prior, with the posterior populations following from a generalised Doob transform. A synthetic time-resolved density with a tenfold slower back-transition lowers {Delta}F from 5.191 to 2.885 kBT , raises the product-basin population from 0.0055 to 0.0529 and slows relaxation 9.47-fold, leaving the reactant basin unchanged. Forward and backward rates accelerated 3 and 20-fold raise {Delta}F by 1.892 kBT and shorten relaxation from 4818 to 289 ps.

papers.title: Membrane Filtration Removes Lipids and Compromises the Acoustic Stability of Nanobubbles
papers.abstract: Nanobubbles (NBs) have been widely investigated as ultrasound contrast and therapeutic agents, yet whether submicron gas bubbles can directly generate measurable ultrasound signals remains controversial. Because acoustic scattering scales with bubble size, several studies have recently attributed nanobubble echogenicity primarily to larger bubbles. A recent Science Advances publication, attributed the loss of ultrasound signal after filtration to the removal of residual larger bubbles [1]. This interpretation assumes that filtration acts solely as a size-selection process. Here, we show that filtration also alters the shell properties and stability of lipid-coated NBs, independent of size. Filtered NBs (F-NBs) show significant lipid loss and accumulation on the filters themselves, resulting in decreased bubble stability and greater susceptibility to destruction under acoustic excitation. To decouple size from processing effects, we generated NB populations size-matched to filtered samples using increased centrifugation (IC-NBs), a comparatively gentler separation method. Despite comparable size distributions, IC-NBs retained sustained ultrasound scattering, whereas filtered NBs showed significantly reduced acoustic persistence. Filtration through 5 m pores, ~5-fold larger than the largest bubbles, preserved acoustic persistence but still reduced bubble concentration by ~30%, suggesting that membrane contact may contribute to bubble loss beyond size exclusion. Complementary lipid and gas-content assays provided further evidence of filtration-induced changes. The 0.45 m filtration removed substantially more total lipid than could be attributed to free-lipid removal alone, while the lipid associated with the larger bubbles removed during filtration accounted for only ~5% of the additional lipid loss. Encapsulated gas content remained comparable to that of size-matched centrifuged controls, suggesting that the reduced acoustic stability of filtered NBs is more closely associated with changes in lipid content than with loss of the gas core. These results indicate that membrane filtration is not a purely size-selective process: it removes substantially more lipid than size exclusion predicts and yields bubbles that are less stable under ultrasound, most likely through changes in shell lipid content or in the surrounding lipid reservoir, underscoring the importance of processing-induced effects in interpreting nanobubble echogenicity.

papers.title: Direct visualization of lysosome-mediated intracellular transport and membrane anchoring of TNF-α in human T cells
papers.abstract: Tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-) represents a major pro-inflammatory cytokine associated with chronic inflammation. Enhanced understanding of intracellular trafficking of TNF- enables the identification of drug targets that modulate TNF- secretion at the cellular source. However, conventional cytokine assays provide only bulk measurements of secreted TNF- or static measurements in fixed cells and therefore cannot provide mechanistic information. Here, we report a fluorescence imaging platform to visualize and quantify intracellular TNF- trafficking in human T cells. Using a Jurkat T cell line stably expressing TNF- fused to mStayGold as a model system, we revealed through single-particle tracking (SPT) that T cell activation increased the motility of TNF- vesicles and that microtubule perturbation disrupted this increased motility. 3D structured illumination microscopy uncovered spatial associations between TNF- vesicles and lysosomes, and SPT further demonstrated their coordinated transport. Using total internal reflection fluorescence microscopy, we captured the sub-second splitting of single TNF- vesicles into multiple puncta that subsequently separated, suggesting delivery of TNF- from the vesicle to the plasma membrane. Confocal-based super-resolution microscopy further resolved TNF- vesicles fusing with the plasma membrane and transmembrane TNF-. Together, these imaging capabilities for tracking and super-resolving the intracellular transport and membrane delivery of TNF- in live T cells enable mechanistic studies of TNF- trafficking and release.

papers.title: Adaptive motility and feeding strategies of deep-branching predatory protists
papers.abstract: Heterotrophic flagellates play a major role in nutrient recycling and shaping aquatic microbial communities. Many motile species have evolved diverse predatory strategies to exploit microbial prey, from bacteria to small eukaryotes. Excavates, deep-branching eukaryotic lineages with distinctive biflagellate morphology and conserved cytoskeletal features, exhibit varied feeding behaviours, including grazing, raptorial feeding, and filter-feeding. However, the temporal dynamics of their motility, feeding, and spatial distribution in relation to bacterial population density remain under-explored. Here, we quantify the behavioural ecology of excavates using high-resolution, single-cell tracking and quantitative analysis. Focussing on two Discoba species - the marine Jakoba libera and freshwater Reclinomonas americana - we identify different behavioural patterns: J. libera swims, forages and feeds, while R. americana swims and feeds. Prey availability differentially affects motility: J. libera increases the number of swimming cells when food is scarce, while R. americana shows the opposite trend. Spatial statistics reveal fundamental differences in their feeding and redistribution strategies. J. libera acts as an active forager, whereas R. americana behaves as a strict filter feeder. A third species, the anaerobic Kipferlia bialata (from a different clade), adopts a foraging strategy similar to J. libera. Together, these results elucidate the adaptive relationship between prey availability, feeding modes, and motility in bacteriovorous excavate flagellates, offering new insights into the ecological and evolutionary dynamics of microbial predators.

papers.title: A permeable G310 constriction limits K+ flux in the activated KCNQ2 pore and is disrupted by the encephalopathy variant G310S
papers.abstract: KCNQ2 (Kv7.2) subunits contribute to the channels that carry the neuronal M-current, and variants in KCNQ2 cause epilepsies that range from self-limited neonatal seizures to developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE). Structures of KCNQ2 bound to PIP2 and cannabidiol show a widened activation gate, yet it has remained unclear which point of the activated pore limits K+ flux and how DEE variants at that point act. We simulated the KCNQ2 pore domain (PDB 8J01) in a POPC bilayer under an applied field of about 565 mV, restraining only the terminal residues of S5 and S6 so that G310 and S314 were free. The activated pore conducted K+ at 4.3 pS (95% CI 2.5-6.9; 17 net filter crossings in 1120 ns over four replicas), while the closed-state pore (PDB 7CR3) conducted none in 560 ns. Conduction proceeded by knock-on through a filter that was doubly occupied in 84-92% of frames. Along S6 the narrowest position of the activated pore was not the canonical gate residue S314 but the glycine of the Pro-Ala-Gly motif, G310: activation widens S314 by 0.37 nm but G310 by only 0.07 nm, and restraining G310 to its closed-state width in one replica abolished gate crossings. The DEE variant G310S reduced conduction about six-fold (G310S/wild-type ratio 0.16, 95% CI 0.02-0.66; p = 0.003). Its serine hydroxyls project into the constriction and halve the water column in the G310 plane (8.7 to 4.7 waters), an effect reproduced in CHARMM36m (9.9 to 4.3). The first coordination shell of a K+ ion at the constriction was, however, conserved (6.3 vs 6.5 oxygens), because the serine hydroxyls replace the waters they displace. The hydroxyls did not retain the ion: contacts lasted tens of picoseconds, and ions were instead turned back at the serine ring, fewer reaching the gate plane (45 vs 79 excursions per microsecond) and fewer of those crossing it (5% vs 23%). In mixed tetramers carrying one or two variant subunits the effect on the water column was additive, each subunit removing about a quarter of it (f = 0.22 and 0.58 of the full effect). These results identify G310 as the flux-limiting constriction of the activated KCNQ2 pore in our simulations and point to a permeation defect as one component of G310S loss of function.

papers.title: Structural Basis for Near Infrared Absorption and Noncanonical Photoisomerization in Neorhodopsin
papers.abstract: In retinal proteins, light absorption leads to a double bond isomerization of the chromophore, followed by conformational relaxations that drive functional protein rearrangements. The balance between photoisomerization and radiative or non-radiative decays of the excited state is adjusted to the demands of the respective photoreceptor function. The molecular determinants controlling the excited state processes remain poorly understood and are the focus of this combined crystallographic, spectroscopic, and theoretical work on the recently discovered neorhodopsin (NeoR). NeoR exhibits a highly red-shifted and fluorescent dark state and selectively photoisomerizes from all-trans to 7-cis. We show that the local electrostatic environment reduces the negative charge density near the Schiff base and suppresses torsional motion around the canonical C13=C14 isomerization site of microbial rhodopsins. Instead, the chromophore-binding pocket permits only low-efficiency C7=C8 isomerization, accompanied by polyene inversion, {beta}-ionone ring displacement, and Schiff base deprotonation. Consequently, unlike other retinal photoreceptors, NeoR undergoes structural changes localized near the {beta}-ionone ring.

papers.title: CryoFAST: A Fab-Aided Cryo-EM Workflow for High-Resolution Structure Determination of Sub-50-kDa Protein Targets
papers.abstract: Single-particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) plays an increasingly important role in structure-based drug discovery (SBDD) by revealing target protein-ligand interactions at the molecular level, but its application has largely focused on large- and medium-sized protein complexes. Many therapeutically important targets are smaller than 50 kDa and remain highly challenging for cryo-EM analysis because of low signal-to-noise ratios and difficulties in particle alignment. Here, we describe cryoFAST, an integrated workflow that couples ligand-compatible Fab discovery and structure-guided computational maturation with biochemical triage, fiducial-complex assembly, and single-particle cryo-EM. Through phage-display screening and/or AI-guided design, we developed high-affinity Fab binders of approximately 50 kDa that stabilize the target without disrupting ligand-target interactions and then assembled Fab-target complexes for cryo-EM analysis. Using the therapeutically relevant extracellular domain (~20 kDa) of interleukin-4 receptor (IL-4R) as a proof of concept, we determined its cryo-EM structure at 2.74 Angstrom resolution and established a framework for elucidating ligand-binding modes. This workflow provides a practical, efficient, and potentially broadly applicable route to the structural characterization of small protein targets that are otherwise challenging to study. By extending the applicability of cryo-EM to high-value but technically challenging small targets, cryoFAST may open new opportunities for structure-based drug discovery.

papers.title: Grow2Fold: mapping heterogeneous developmental growth to human brain folding
papers.abstract: Cortical folding emerges through complex developmental processes, yet what organizes these processes into the characteristic folding patterns of the human brain remains unclear. Here, we developed an imaging-informed whole-brain modeling framework, Grow2Fold, that integrates developmental cortical regionalization, quantitative growth characterization, and mechanics-guided simulation to investigate how cortical growth shapes brain folding patterns. Using 836 fetal and neonatal MRI sessions from 747 participants spanning 21-45 postmenstrual weeks, we identified a reproducible and hierarchical spatiotemporal organization of cortical expansion characterized by coordinated regional growth trajectories. Rapid expansion occurs earlier around peri-central territories and progressively shifts toward frontal, parietal, and temporal association cortices. We encoded these imaging-derived trajectories into region- and age-specific growth laws and incorporated them into anatomically realistic whole-brain mechanical models. The resulting simulations recapitulate major sulcal landmarks and characteristic folding development across global and regional morphological measures. Comparing regional and uniform growth, we find that differential growth drives cortical instability, while heterogeneous developmental growth organizes this instability into anatomically recognizable folding patterns. Combined with subject-specific anatomy, these population-informed growth laws reproduce individualized longitudinal folding trajectories. Together, our results identify spatiotemporally patterned developmental growth as a key spatial constraint on cortical morphogenesis and establish a quantitative bridge from developmental imaging, through mechanical instability, to anatomically organized folding.
